package_info.package_name: N/A (RepoJacking vulnerability affects any package using a renamed GitHub username)
package_info.package_manager: Go, Swift, Packagist (and any manager using GitHub URLs as source)
package_info.package_versions: All versions referencing vulnerable (renamed) GitHub repositories
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerability allows attackers to hijack the namespace of popular repositories after a username change, enabling them to serve malicious code to users who depend on the original repository. This is a supply chain attack vector that can poison packages and GitHub Actions at scale.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original under a reclaimed username, then pushes malicious code.
malicious_snippets.code_language: any (depends on original repository language, e.g., Go, PHP, Swift, YAML for GitHub Actions)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When users or package managers fetch or install from the hijacked repository URL, they receive attacker-controlled (potentially malicious) code instead of the original code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hijacking a popular repository namespace to serve different code than expected is a classic supply chain attack.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Users expect the repository URL to always point to the original, trusted code. Instead, it can silently point to attacker code after a username rename and RepoJacking.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate repository transfers or username changes, but never with the intent to deceive or serve malicious code.
key_indicators: Repository at a previously retired namespace suddenly reappears with different commit history
Code changes that introduce unexpected or obfuscated logic
Repository owner history shows recent username rename and transfer activity

attack_chain.action: Attacker registers a GitHub username that was previously used by a popular repository owner who renamed their account.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can now create a repository with the same name as the original under the reclaimed username.

attack_chain.action: Attacker creates a repository with the same name as the original (e.g., 'repo') under the hijacked username.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository URL now points to attacker-controlled code.

attack_chain.action: Attacker pushes malicious code to the new repository.
attack_chain.leads_to: Any user or package manager fetching from the original URL receives malicious code.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code is distributed to users via package managers or direct git clone/install commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential compromise of user systems, supply chain poisoning, or further attacks.

behavioral_signatures: Repository at a previously retired namespace reappears with a new owner
Sudden changes in repository commit history or codebase at a popular namespace
Repository owner history shows recent username rename and transfer activity
file_indicators: Repository files at a namespace that was previously retired
Unexpected or obfuscated code in newly created repositories at popular namespaces
network_indicators: Package manager or CI/CD systems fetching code from a namespace with recent ownership changes
Unusual spikes in downloads or clones from a newly created repository at a popular namespace
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for the recreation of repositories at previously retired namespaces, especially following a username rename. Alert on any repository that appears at a namespace with a history of high popularity but a new owner. Compare commit histories and codebases for significant, unexplained changes. Package managers and CI/CD systems should validate repository owner history and consider using immutable commit hashes or new package URLs rather than relying on username/repo combinations.
